description: Table 1, a five-column literature-summary table rendered as an image, titled "Summary of corrosion-related literature on LDSs." The column headers are Materials, Treatment, Phenomenon, Mechanism and Ref. Eight rows survey Fe-Mn-Al-C low-density steels (LDSs) and the effect of microalloying additions on corrosion behaviour. Row 1: Fe-xMn-3Al-3Si with + 21-28 % Mn shows reduced polarization resistance and increased corrosion current density, attributed to excess Mn causing insufficient Al enrichment in the oxide films (Ref. [12]). Row 2: Fe-25Mn-10Al-1.5 C with + 2 % Cr, + 2 % Ni shows increased OCP and polarization resistance and reduced corrosion rate (Ref. [13]). Row 3: Fe-30Mn-10.5Al-1.1 C with + 3 % Cr, + 3 % Mo shows increased pitting potential (Ref. [20]). Row 4: Fe-30Mn-8Al-1.2 C with + 2 % Cr, + 2 % Mo shows decreased corrosion current density (Ref. [21]). Row 5: Fe-19Mn-12Al-1.5 C with + 5 % Cr shows increased pitting potential but reduced film thickness (Ref. [22]). Row 6: Fe-30Mn-8Al-1C with + 3 % Cu shows increased carbide formation and accelerated corrosion rate (Ref. [23]). Row 7: Fe-21Mn-10Al-1.25 C with + 3 % Ni shows increased corrosion rate via B2 phase at GBs (Ref. [24]). Row 8: Fe-20Mn-11.5Al-1.4 C with + 5 % Cr shows higher pitting potential compared with stainless steel (Ref. [25]). The table makes no numeric property values printed; it tabulates qualitative directions of change plus mechanisms, arguing that Cr, Mo and Ni additions improve passive-film protectiveness while Mn and Cu are detrimental.

observations.observation: The table has five columns headed Materials, Treatment, Phenomenon, Mechanism and Ref., and contains eight data rows.

Row 1 lists alloy Fe-xMn-3Al-3Si treated with + 21-28 % Mn, showing reduced polarization resistance and increased corrosion current density, with mechanism 'Excess Mn content leaded to insufficient Al enrichment in the oxide films', Ref. [12].
Row 2 lists Fe-25Mn-10Al-1.5 C with + 2 % Cr, + 2 % Ni, showing increased OCP and polarization resistance and reduced corrosion rate, Ref. [13].
Row 3 lists Fe-30Mn-10.5Al-1.1 C with + 3 % Cr, + 3 % Mo, showing increased pitting potential, Ref. [20].
Row 4 lists Fe-30Mn-8Al-1.2 C with + 2 % Cr, + 2 % Mo, showing decreased corrosion current density, Ref. [21].
Row 5 lists Fe-19Mn-12Al-1.5 C with + 5 % Cr, showing increased pitting potential but reduced film thickness, Ref. [22].

Row 6 lists Fe-30Mn-8Al-1C with + 3 % Cu, showing increased carbide formation and accelerated corrosion rate, mechanism 'Cu enriched at the GBs and combined with dissolved oxygen to form an unstable oxide film', Ref. [23].
Row 7 lists Fe-21Mn-10Al-1.25 C with + 3 % Ni, showing increased corrosion rate, mechanism 'B2 phase at GBs enhanced microgalvanic corrosion, leading to inhomogeneous film', Ref. [24].
Row 8 lists Fe-20Mn-11.5Al-1.4 C with + 5 % Cr, showing higher pitting potential compared with stainless steel and passive films thicker than stainless steel with higher Cr+Al contents, Ref. [25].
No numeric corrosion property values (current density, potential, rate) are printed in the table; only directions of change (increased/decreased) are given.
The caption states the table is a summary of corrosion-related literature on LDSs.

The citing text states that higher Mn content in steel increases the proportion of weakly protective Mn oxides in the corrosion product film, deteriorating corrosion resistance [11-14], consistent with row 1 of the table.

The citing text states that adding Cr, Mo and Ni promotes enrichment of beneficial elements (Al, Cr, Mo) in the passive film, increases its thickness and reduces defect density, improving film stability and pitting resistance; Table 1 is cited as summarising these studies [12,13,20-25].

measured_quantities: OCP (open circuit potential, qualitative direction only)
